title: FreshCart: should a grocer sell meal kits?
prompt: Our client is FreshCart, a regional grocery chain with 50 stores in the Southeast. The CEO wants to know whether FreshCart should start selling meal kits, and if so, how.

clarifying_answers.objective: Grow profit and give loyal shoppers a reason to visit more often.
clarifying_answers.format: In-store kits on a shelf, with optional pre-order through the FreshCart app. No home delivery.
clarifying_answers.geography: FreshCart's current stores in the Southeast.

hidden_facts.hint: customer demand, surveys, or how often people would buy
hidden_facts.fact: In a survey, 15% of loyalty households said they would buy a meal kit about twice a month.

hidden_facts.hint: price, cost, or margin per kit
hidden_facts.fact: An in-store meal kit would sell for $25 and cost $17 to make, including food, packaging, and labor.
HelloFresh and Home Chef charge about $10 to $12 per serving, delivered. 2 rival grocery chains already sell in-store kits, and one dropped them after a year because of food waste.

hidden_facts.hint: food waste, spoilage, or unsold product
hidden_facts.fact: Prepared foods at FreshCart waste about 10% of the items made.

math_answers.question: How many kits a year could FreshCart sell (in thousands)?
What gross profit would that earn before waste?
What is gross profit after accounting for waste?

ideal_structure: Market and customers: demand among FreshCart shoppers
Economics: kits x margin, minus waste
Competition: delivery kits vs in-store rivals
Entry plan: pilot, pre-orders to cut waste
recommendation: Yes, through a pilot. At full scale FreshCart could sell about 1.4 million kits a year and earn about $9M in gross profit after waste. Waste is the reason a rival quit, so launch in about 10 stores with app pre-orders to forecast demand, then expand if waste stays under 10%.
common_mistakes: Ignoring waste even though a competitor failed because of it
Comparing on price with delivery kits instead of convenience
